meta.regime: The regime has resolved from a four-way tightening race into a single clear leader. For three weeks this board has been compressed, with four central banks hiking inside eight days and every one of those hikes already priced, so being a tightening central bank bought a currency nothing. Last night broke the tie: Japan printed the fastest nominal wage growth since 1997 with real wages positive for a seventh month, which removed the one genuine objection to the BoJ path and made September 18 a formality rather than a question. At the same time Fed pricing drifted back toward a coin flip. The yen is now the only currency on this board with both a locked catalyst and a repaired domestic story, and the trade is to own it against the two currencies that have neither - sterling and the kiwi.
meta.nextBigEvent: US August CPI on Friday September 11 at 12:30Z, headline consensus 3.4%, with PPI the day before at 12:30Z. dailyRead: The print this file has been pointing at for a week landed overnight, and it landed on the strong side by a distance. Japan's average cash earnings rose 4.7% year-on-year in July against a 3.9% consensus and a 4.0% prior - the fastest nominal wage growth since 1997 - with average monthly pay per worker at 436,401 yen and special earnings up 6.3% as this year's shunto settlements fed through. More important than the nominal number is the real one: real wages rose 2.4% year-on-year, the biggest increase since May 2021 and the SEVENTH consecutive month of gains, and the labour-ministry deflator moved above 2% for the first time this year, meaning wages beat an inflation rate that is itself accelerating. Yesterday's file named this print as the single thing that would take JPY from +2 to +1. It did the reverse, and it did something more than that - it retired the standing caveat. This file has argued for weeks that the BoJ was hiking into an oil shock that strengthened its inflation argument while eroding its demand base, citing eight consecutive monthly falls in real household spending, a trade balance at MINUS 634 billion yen and a current account at MINUS 92.3 billion. Two of those three legs broke overnight in Japan's favour: the current account swung to PLUS 2,989 billion yen, and retail sales printed +2.4% month-on-month after -3.9%. Seven straight months of rising real wages is the definition of a demand base being repaired rather than eroded. Pricing responded accordingly - September 18 is now effectively FULLY priced for a hike to 1.25%, which is also TE's own forecast, and USD/JPY fell to 153.931, its lowest since February 18, down 0.28% on the session, 3.92% on the WEEK and 3.39% on the month. JPY goes to +3. That is the first top score this file has assigned, and it is warranted because the yen is now the only currency on this board carrying a locked catalyst, a repaired domestic story and a bond market whose rise in yields is read as policy normalisation rather than fiscal stress - the 10-year at 3% for the first time since 1996. Board member Takata's argument that the Bank should move NIMBLY, faster or in larger increments than its semiannual pace, is still the underpriced part: the market has one 25bp step in the price, not a Bank that accelerates. The second change is the dollar, and it is a change in PRICING rather than in data. This file has been carrying CME FedWatch at roughly 66% for September 16, a level set on August 31 immediately after Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole remarks. It has since drifted materially: the current read is roughly a coin flip, with one tracker showing 49.4% for a 25bp hike against 50.6% for a hold, down from 57% a week ago, and other measures nearer 60%. Nothing in the US data deteriorated - August payrolls at +162,000 with 55,000 of upward revisions still stand, unemployment is 4.1%, CPI 3.4% with the monthly rate at 0.1%, GDP 2.1% annual, non-manufacturing PMI 55.4 and services 56.5 - so the dollar HOLDS at +1 rather than being cut. But the practical consequence is that the USD/JPY differential widened from BOTH ends at once, a fully-priced BoJ against a Fed that is no longer two-thirds priced, and that is why USD/JPY is upgraded from MEDIUM to HIGH despite CPI sitting three days away. DXY is 98.939, down 0.24% on the session and 0.74% on the week. The third change is the kiwi, and it is a downgrade. NZD/USD is 0.58463, down 0.52% and the weakest major on the board today, falling for a THIRD consecutive session. The evidence behind it is not one number but four: Chinese imports rose 28.2% year-on-year against a 30% consensus, and China is New Zealand's largest trading partner; ANZ business confidence slipped to 53.7 from 56.1; the manufacturing PMI collapsed to 54.3 from 60.1; and consumer confidence fell to 80.4 from 94.7. Set that against an RBNZ which hiked to 2.75% on September 2 and then explicitly said it was gradually REMOVING stimulus while attributing 4.1% inflation largely to Middle East fuel prices, with TE showing October 28 unchanged and only December at 3.00%. A central bank looking through its own CPI, plus four separate sentiment deteriorations, plus a China miss, is a currency going to MINUS 1. It now sits level with sterling at the bottom. Sterling itself HOLDS at -1, and honesty requires saying which leg of yesterday's downgrade has softened. The acute one has: after 10-year gilts hit 5.294% - the highest since June 2008 - and the 30-year reached 5.904%, the highest since 1998, the bond market CALMED from September 3, and cable at 1.35286 is actually up 0.08% on the week and 0.14% on the month. So the gilt move is no longer accelerating. What has not changed is the structural half, and it is the more durable half: the UK carries the highest borrowing costs of any G10 developed nation, government borrowing in July ran 69% above the prior year, public sector debt is close to 95% of GDP with debt interest alone above 100 billion pounds a year, and a 48bp yield advantage over Treasuries is failing to attract capital precisely because it is a risk premium rather than carry. Add a Bank of England roughly 90% priced to hold at 3.75% on September 17 after the DMP survey cut one-year firm CPI expectations to 3.1%, UK core CPI flat at 2.6%, wage growth decelerating to 4.1% and quarterly GDP at +0.4% from +0.6%, and sterling stays the funding leg - just with one fast-moving reason replaced by one slow-moving one. The euro is the interesting hold. Eurostat revised Q2 GDP UP on September 7: +0.6% quarter-on-quarter against +0.4% previously and 1.2% year-on-year against 0.6%, with Germany lifted to 0.3% from 0.2% and Ireland to 10.2% from 3.9%, though France was cut to 0.0%. That is a genuine improvement two days before the ECB and it is tempting to reverse yesterday's downgrade. It should not be reversed, and the reason is precise: yesterday's cut from +2 to +1 was not about euro-area growth, it was about the September 3 Reuters poll in which all 65 economists expect Thursday's 25bp to 2.50% while 91% then see 2.50% as the year-END rate and 78% see it held through mid-2027. A GDP revision does not reopen a forward path that economists have closed. What it does do is put a floor under Thursday - a Lagarde press conference is now much less likely to sound dovish with growth revised up and HICP at 3.3%, the highest since September 2023. So EUR holds +1, own it against sterling and the kiwi where the differential is structural, and leave EUR/USD, EUR/CAD and EUR/CHF as ranges. Australia holds +2 and gets a cleaner commodity leg than it has had in a month. Copper is 6.7175 USD per pound on TE, up 1.83% on the session and 3.16% on the week, at record levels in tonne terms, and the driver is SUPPLY rather than Chinese demand - Codelco and Freeport-McMoRan both posted double-digit production declines, the ICSG recorded a 1.1% fall in global production in the first half, and there is an export ban in Congo alongside weak Chilean and Peruvian output. That matters for the honest version of the Aussie case: it is a terms-of-trade positive regardless of cause, so the flat-copper drag this file has carried is retired, but it is not the China demand recovery the AUD bulls want, and the same China trade release that hurt the kiwi applies here too. The domestic picture is mixed in the same way - the cash rate is 4.35%, the G10 high, trimmed mean stuck at 3.6%, the monthly inflation rate jumped +1.0% from -0.1%, and Q2 growth at 2.1% annual remains above the RBA's estimated 2% speed limit; against that, consumer confidence fell to 84.4 from 88.9 and business confidence to -8 from -6. September 29 sits near 54%. Canada holds +1 and the split narrowed in its favour. The oil leg is stronger again with WTI at 93.747, up 2.48% today, 3.93% on the week and 14.17% on the month at a six-week high, and two other things improved: the current account swung to PLUS C$8,800 million from MINUS 8,300, and business confidence jumped to 64.3 from 55.1 with Q2 growth annualising at 3.3%. The jobs leg is still the broken one - employment MINUS 41,700 in August with wage growth decelerating to 2.0% year-on-year - and the C$27.6 billion of counter-tariffs took effect yesterday. Switzerland holds +1 with a strong manufacturing PMI at 57.1 from 53.2 and a current account at 15,544 million francs, but the SNB's stated readiness to intervene keeps every franc cross at MEDIUM or below. Finally the war, which escalated in both directions. Iran's Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei has now formally announced the restricted zone, running from the US naval blockade line through the Strait and into the Persian Gulf, with ships entering without coordination to be added to Iran's sanctions list, affecting their insurance and future passage. More significantly, Iran RETALIATED militarily: after US Central Command struck three Iranian tankers near Kharg Island, in the Jask region and in the Gulf of Oman, Iranian forces struck three US-affiliated tankers inside the Strait itself, and the IRGC fired ballistic missiles at a US carrier and destroyer. Transits are running above nine million barrels a day against roughly twenty million before the conflict. Brent is 98.376 and WTI 93.747, both at six-week highs. USOIL is upgraded to HIGH.

geopolitics: The war escalated in both directions overnight and the oil price finally broke to a six-week high on it. The physical exchange is now two-sided: US Central Command struck three Iranian oil tankers - near Kharg Island, in the Jask region and in the Gulf of Oman - and Iranian forces retaliated by striking three US-affiliated tankers INSIDE the Strait of Hormuz, while the IRGC fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer. Alongside that, Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei formally announced the restricted zone this file has been flagging as pending: it runs from the line where the US naval blockade begins, through the Strait, and into the Persian Gulf on the far side, and ships identified as entering it without coordinating with Tehran will be added to Iran's sanctions list - a designation that affects their insurance cover and their future passage. WTI is 93.747, up 2.48% on the session, 3.93% on the week and 14.17% on the month; Brent is 98.376 after an intraday 98.06 on Monday. The countervailing fact, and the reason this is not a limitless rally, is that transits are still running above nine million barrels a day against roughly twenty million before the conflict, so a large part of the disruption is already in the price, the US has cleared the strait of mines and materially degraded Iran's ability to re-lay them, and workarounds keep expanding. Even so, the combination of a formal legal-economic instrument and actual retaliatory strikes on shipping is enough to upgrade USOIL from MEDIUM to HIGH. Six FX consequences follow. First, and most important today, the transmission to the YEN has inverted. For weeks this file argued that Japan's terms of trade were the weak half of the yen case - it imports essentially all its oil, the trade balance was MINUS 634 billion yen and the current account MINUS 92.3 billion. That argument is much weaker this morning: the current account swung to PLUS 2,989 billion yen, retail sales printed +2.4% month-on-month, and real wages rose 2.4% for a seventh consecutive month, meaning Japanese households are absorbing the energy shock rather than being crushed by it. The BoJ is now hiking into an oil shock that strengthens its inflation argument WITHOUT the demand offset, which is precisely why JPY goes to +3 and the trade balance is the only leg of the old caveat still standing. Second, Canada is the direct beneficiary and its case broadened today - crude at a six-week high, the current account swinging to PLUS C$8,800 million, business confidence jumping to 64.3 from 55.1, and Q2 growth annualising at 3.3% - though the labour market with employment down 41,700 and wages at 2.0% keeps CAD at +1 rather than higher. Third, the tightening board still rests on this one shock and the central banks say so explicitly: the RBA's August minutes list Middle East conflict driving oil prices FIRST among the arguments for a hike, the BoC's September statement flags the continuation of the war as an upside inflation risk, the RBNZ attributes its 4.1% inflation largely to Middle East fuel prices, and the ECB accounts cite Middle East upside risk. Four reaction functions from one input - which is also why the whole board would reprice together on a de-escalation. Fourth, the franc ceiling becomes more relevant rather than less: a haven bid into a formally declared restricted zone is exactly the scenario the SNB described in June when it signalled greater readiness to intervene, so CHF stays capped at +1 and every franc cross stays at MEDIUM or below despite a manufacturing PMI at 57.1 and a current account at 15,544 million. Fifth, the European gas channel is quietly getting worse and it is the sterling problem the market is underweighting: EU gas is 75.15 euros per MWh and up 24.40% on the month, German gas is up 19.86%, and UK gas is up 25.12% into a confirmed October Ofgem cap rise - which is simultaneously the one residual hawkish argument for the Bank of England and a direct drag on GER40. Sixth, the bond-market distinction that drove yesterday's sterling downgrade still holds but has cooled on one side: gilts calmed from September 3 after peaking at 5.294% on the 10-year and 5.904% on the 30-year, so the acute UK leg is no longer accelerating, while Japan's 10-year at 3% continues to read as normalisation. The UK's structural fiscal premium - the highest borrowing costs in G10, July borrowing 69% above the prior year, debt near 95% of GDP - is what keeps sterling negative now that the fast-moving part has stopped moving.
